transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Solutions), Evan Martin (CTO, Stratiform), Leila Ortiz (SRE), Marco Ruiz (Product), Dana Cho (Infra)

Summary (auto): quick discovery to map p95 latency targets, concurrency and streaming behavior across hosted/dedicated/private options. Customer wants token/sec burst sizing and fallback strategy.

[00:00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:00:05] Evan: yep loud and clear, thanks.
[00:00:07] Jordan: cool i'll kick off — quick agenda: understand your traffic, p95 SLOs, whether streaming is required end-to-end, and then go over hosting modes and a proposed benchmark plan.
[00:00:20] Leila: sounds good, we wanna figure out whether we go hosted for Q1 pilot or go straight to dedicated. main constraint is p95 under 250ms for our shortest path, and overall token/sec for bursts of up to 6k tokens/sec for a minute.
[00:00:33] Priya: got it, when you say 250ms p95 is that end-to-end from client or from your service to inference?
[00:00:38] Leila: from our API gateway to the generated token stream arriving at the client. includes network hop, so we assume ~30–50ms network overhead.
[00:00:47] Marco: And streamable responses are important for our chat product — we do token streaming to the front end. cold start behavior matters too, we can't have 2s stalls frequently.
[00:00:58] Jordan: ok that's helpful. can you talk about concurrency patterns — are bursts many short requests or long sequences?
[00:01:05] Evan: mixture — about 70% are short prompt completions (avg 40 tokens output), 20% mid-length (200–600 tokens), 10% long-form (2k+). Peak concurrency is expected during campaign launches — around 200 concurrent streams, but short ones can spike to 800 concurrent short calls for 30–90s.
[00:01:24] Priya: that helps. for Redwood Dedicated we can size GPU pools for steady-state plus burst queueing, and streaming concurrency is a different resource profile because of KV cache memory — long sequences use more memory and affect throughput.
[00:01:37] Dana: question — if we went hosted, would you be able to guarantee isolation and predictable p95 during those 800-concurrent short spikes?
[00:01:45] Jordan: hosted has tenancy isolation at the request layer but not physical GPU isolation; we rely on smart routing and reserved burst capacity for higher tiers. dedicated gives you the predictability — you get dedicated GPU pools. there is also Redwood Private (VPC) if you want network-level isolation.
[00:01:58] Evan: cost is a concern though. Dedicated sounds expensive if we need to provision for peak spikes that happen a few times a month.
[00:02:06] Samir: totally — that's where autoscaling + burst policies and smart routing help. we can size for steady-state and provide burst nodes that spin up with a warm cache profile; plus prefix/KV caching reduces token compute for common prompts.
[00:02:18] Leila: you mentioned KV cache — can you explain memory implications for streaming long sequences? our long form runs into GPU memory primarily.
[00:02:25] Priya: sure — KV cache is per request and grows with sequence length. on some model variants we can use quantized attention kernels which lowers memory per token and allows more concurrent long streams per GPU. but it's model-dependent. in our tests for a 13B model quantized we saw ~30% more concurrency vs fp16.
[00:02:44] Marco: did you mean 30% or 3%?
[00:02:46] Priya: 30%, typo — 30% more concurrency.
[00:02:48] Evan: what's the expected p95 per-token latency at that config?
[00:02:52] Priya: ballpark for streaming token output on a 13B quantized model is 6–12ms/token in ideal cases; p95 depends on batch formation and queueing. for short prompts p95 can be under 200ms end to end if network adds ~40ms. for long-form it's more about tail from memory pressure.
[00:03:08] Leila: interesting. our target for short path is 250ms p95, so sounds feasible. what about cold starts causing spikes?
[00:03:15] Samir: cold starts are mitigated with warm pools and prefix caching. Dedicated is easiest to control for cold starts because you keep a pool hot; hosted uses warm standby instances depending on plan.
[00:03:25] Dana: we need SOC2 and audit logs, SSO/SAML — can hosted meet those?
[00:03:30] Jordan: yes, hosted has SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, audit logs; private can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for encryption-at-rest keys. I'll attach the security pack.
[00:03:41] Evan: when you say audit logs, are they token-level or only request-level?
[00:03:45] Jordan: request-level and metadata. we can push more detailed telemetry into your observability pipeline on Dedicated/Private with a data-forwarding option.
[00:03:53] Leila: what about quantization/regression risks — we need consistent quality, can't accept hallucination delta when we change model variants for performance.
[00:03:59] Priya: under Redwood Optimize we run quality/regression checks tied to prompt sets. for any quantized variant we can run your golden prompt set and give acceptance thresholds before rollout.
[00:04:10] Marco: cool. let's talk benchmarking — what would you need from us to run a realistic token/sec and p95 benchmark?
[00:04:16] Priya: sample traffic profile (distribution of lengths, concurrency over time), 3–5 representative prompts, target model family, and whether you require streaming semantics. also expected peak duration.
[00:04:26] Evan: we can provide that. how long does a bench take and how do results differ between hosted and dedicated?
[00:04:30] Samir: typical bench run is 4–8 hours to capture warm/cold behavior; short smoke test can be a few hours. hosted shows multi-tenant variability — we measure median and p95 under simulated noisy neighbors. Dedicated gives near-deterministic p95 curves. we produce token/sec throughput vs p95 charts.
[00:04:47] Leila: can you give a simple example — if we target p95=250ms for 40-token outputs at 800 concurrent short calls, what does that map to for GPUs? ballpark numbers?
[00:04:58] Priya: rough back-of-envelope: for 800 concurrent 40-token short calls that's about 32k tokens outstanding across the cluster during the spike. On a modern A100-ish or H100-like node with optimized kernels you might get ~6–12k tokens/sec per GPU for short token generation depending on model. So you'd need ~3–6 GPUs to handle the peak in steady streaming throughput, but concurrency and cold starts push that up — recommended to have headroom and either burst nodes or queueing.
[00:05:21] Jordan: important to note those numbers vary by model flavor and quantization. we'll run a representative bench and give a recommended pool size and expected p95 at that pool size.
[00:05:29] Evan: ok. and cost tradeoffs? Dedicated monthly commit vs hosted variable billing?
[00:05:34] Jordan: hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is committed with a lower per-token cost for heavy steady traffic. we can show you TCO models for your projected monthly tokens.
[00:05:42] Marco: do you support multi-region failover for user geos? we have EU customers and need sub-300ms p95 there too.
[00:05:48] Samir: yes, we can deploy dedicated pools in regions; hosted has global routing. we can set routing policies per region and have automatic fallback to compatible model variants in another region if capacity constrained.
[00:05:58] Leila: last technical: what observability do we get for p95 breakdown — token-level vs queueing vs network?
[00:06:04] Priya: Redwood Console provides per-route token and latency breakdown, tail traces, and model-level breakdowns. We'll enable tracing hooks for a sample route so you can attribute p95 to queueing, kernel time, or network.
[00:06:14] Evan: great. i think next steps are clear. can you propose a short pilot that exercises short spikes and long-form streaming?
[00:06:20] Jordan: yes — propose a 2-week pilot: week 1 smoke tests on hosted + dedicated small pool, week 2 a 48-hour peak spike run with your traffic.
[00:06:29] Marco: timeline sounds reasonable. we'll try to have traffic samples by Wednesday.
[00:06:33] Dana: any infra access required for the dedicated test?
[00:06:35] Priya: minimal — for hosted we just need API keys and traffic generator. for dedicated/Private we need peering info or temporary VPN creds if you want VPC testing. we'll send an access checklist.
[00:06:45] Jordan: recap — Jordan sends pricing + security pack; Priya sends bench plan and access checklist; Evan provides traffic sample and key prompts. We'll sync next Thursday to review pilot plan.
[00:06:56] Evan: thanks everyone.
[00:06:57] Leila: thanks.

Notes / Observations:
- Customer prioritizes sub-250ms p95 for short path and streaming delivery.
- Traffic is skewed to short prompts but peaks cause very high concurrency; careful capacity/burst planning needed.
- Hosted could work for initial pilot but Dedicated recommended for deterministic p95 and cold start control.
- Security/compliance ok with hosted but Private desired if KMS/HSM integration or network isolation is required.

Referenced artifacts:
- Redwood hosted vs dedicated pricing deck (link: sent post-call)

End of transcript.
